conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician here. I’m so glad you came in today; the first weeks and months with a new baby can be a huge adjustment, and it’s completely normal to have lots of feelings during this time.

To help us understand how you’ve been doing, I’d like to use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s just 10 questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of how “good” a mom you are—there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you today.

Everything you share is confidential and stays between you and our team. If any answers suggest you might need extra support, we’ll talk together about gentle next steps. We’ll go at your pace, and you can pause or skip anything that feels uncomfortable.

Shall we begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Hmm… I guess most of the time I can still laugh, just maybe not as easily as before the baby. Like, if my partner makes a joke or something silly happens, I’ll chuckle, but it doesn’t feel quite as light-hearted as it used to. Maybe three or four days out of the week I’ll genuinely laugh; the other days I’m just too tired or preoccupied.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I still manage to laugh—maybe not quite as hard or as often as before the baby, but usually once or twice a day something will make me smile.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do still look forward to some things—like my morning coffee or when my mom comes over to hold the baby so I can shower—but it’s not the same excitement I used to feel. It’s more like “I guess that’ll be nice” instead of really counting down the minutes.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was fussy for hours and I kept thinking maybe my milk wasn’t “good enough” or I’d done something wrong at bedtime. Rationally I know babies just cry, but I still go straight to “this is my fault.” It’s not every single time, but probably most days I’ll find something to beat myself up over.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes. Like, I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing when he’s napping, even though the monitor looks fine. It’s not constant—maybe a couple of times a day—and I can usually talk myself down pretty quickly, but it still pops up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—just that quick little jolt of “what-if” when I check the crib. It’s gone in a minute, and I can settle myself, so I wouldn’t call it scared or panicky exactly.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When the baby won’t settle and the laundry’s piled up, it feels like I’m drowning a bit. I usually get through it, but I’ve had maybe two or three moments this week where I just had to put him in the crib for five minutes and walk away to breathe.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, sleeping itself isn’t the problem—I’m tired enough that once the baby and I are both down I usually nod off. It’s just that sometimes my thoughts keep swirling—did I sterilize the bottles, is he gaining enough weight—and it takes me maybe 20 minutes longer to drift off, but I still get a decent stretch.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I do feel kind of down some days—like a heaviness that sits on me, especially in the late afternoon when I’m running on empty. It’s not all day, and it lifts a bit when my partner gets home or when the baby gives me a smile, but it’s definitely there more often than I’d like.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I cried twice this week—once when the baby wouldn’t latch and once when I dropped a plate and it shattered. Both times I felt silly right afterward, but yeah, the tears just came.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never—nothing like that.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item self-report (EPDS-style) plus clarifying comments; 2–3 wk postpartum.

Symptoms endorsed (frequency & severity):
- Depressed mood: “heaviness... more often than I’d like,” worse late-afternoon, improves with support.
- Anhedonia: reduced enjoyment; anticipatory pleasure “not the same excitement.”
- Excessive guilt / self-blame: most days; attributes infant fussiness to personal failure.
- Tearfulness: two crying episodes this week over minor triggers.
- Overwhelm: 2–3 instances of needing to place infant in crib and “walk away to breathe.”
- Transient, situational anxiety: 2× daily “what-if” spikes re: infant breathing; self-soothes within minutes.
- Mild initial insomnia: 20-min sleep-onset delay due to racing thoughts; no middle/late insomnia.

Symptoms denied:
- Panic attacks, persistent panic state.
- Middle-/late-insomnia linked to low mood.
- Any self-harm or suicidal ideation.

Pattern: Sub-syndromal depressive and anxiety symptoms in context of infant care stress; no safety concerns at present.

Screening significance: Meets partial criteria for minor/major depressive episode and/or generalized anxiety; does not meet threshold for high-intensity intervention but warrants close monitoring, psycho-education, and possible outpatient counseling.

Next steps discussed: Re-screen in 2 weeks; safety plan reviewed; advised to contact provider sooner if mood worsens, functioning declines, or any thoughts of self-harm emerge.
